messages.html.008: Explore annual and monthly histories with their original units and definitions.
messages.html.039: From monthly prices to interpreting indicators: concepts from Louis Tomczyk’s document, with formulas and examples.
messages.html.041: One period corresponds to one month. A short window reacts faster; a longer window smooths fluctuations more strongly.
messages.html.042: Settings apply to all assets for this session.
messages.html.045: Fixed settings: SMA 12 and 24 months · EMA 12 and 26 months · MACD signal 9 months · Bollinger ± 2 standard deviations.
messages.html.049: Let Pt denote the price in month t. Observations are monthly: windows of 12 or 26 periods therefore refer to months, not days. Data are sorted chronologically before any calculations.
messages.html.051: The document introduces gold prices and cites INSEE as its source. The original CSV files already go back to 1990. The application now includes four verified INSEE histories, from January 1990 to July 2026, with explicit units.
messages.html.053: Price retains the original values. Base 100 sets the first visible price to 100: reaching 120 means a 20% increase. The logarithmic axis retains prices and their units, with spacing proportional to their logarithm. Proportional changes become comparable: a doubling always spans the same vertical distance.
messages.html.054:
Base 100t = 100 × Pt / P0
Gold / silver ratiot = Pgold,t / Psilver,t
messages.html.055: The ratio uses months shared by both series, in dollars per troy ounce. The original copper CSV duplicates gold; the built-in series now uses official copper prices.
messages.html.060: This is the relative change between two months. Moving from 100 to 105 gives 0.05, or +5%. Simple returns compound by multiplication; they do not add together.
messages.html.063:
ℓt = ln(Pt / Pt−1)
Σ ℓt = ln(PT / P0)
messages.html.064: Close to the simple return for small changes, it adds exactly over time. The application uses it to calculate volatility. Prices must be strictly positive.
messages.html.067: This formula describes exactly the same monthly return repeated for 12 months. Applied to an arithmetic mean of variable returns, it does not recover the actual compounded growth. The “Annualised return” card therefore displays CAGR, defined below.
messages.html.072: Each observation carries equal weight. SMA smooths fluctuations; a price above its average is high relative to the last n months. The 12- and 24-month curves provide two time horizons, with a lag inherent in smoothing.
messages.html.075: Recent observations carry more weight. The smaller n, the larger α and the more responsive the EMA. Like a low-pass filter in signal processing, it attenuates rapid oscillations while tracking the trend. The application compares 12- and 26-month EMAs.
messages.html.076: With n = 3, α = 0.5. If the previous EMA is 100 and the new price is 110, the EMA becomes 105. Moving-average crossovers describe past changes in trend; they can become frequent in a directionless market.
messages.html.078:
Centre = SMAn(P)
Upper band = Centre + 2 sn(P)
Lower band = Centre − 2 sn(P)
messages.html.079: The default window is 20 months. Here, s is the sample standard deviation of prices in the window, using the divisor n − 1. Wider bands indicate greater price dispersion around the local average.
messages.html.080: Crossing a band places the price far from this average; it does not guarantee an immediate return to the centre. The bands do not automatically form a 95% probability interval.
messages.html.083: Momentum describes price movement. A basic measure is M<sub>t</sub> = P<sub>t</sub> − P<sub>t−k</sub>. MACD and RSI provide two complementary views of these dynamics.
messages.html.084: MACD · Moving average convergence and divergence
messages.html.085:
MACD = EMA12(P) − EMA26(P)
Signal = EMA9(MACD)
Histogram = MACD − Signal
messages.html.086: A positive MACD means the short EMA is above the long EMA; a negative MACD means the opposite. The signal line smooths MACD. A positive histogram places MACD above its signal; if it rises, the gap is widening. This is a difference between two curves, not an exact derivative of price. The application plots this difference as a time-series curve; its conventional name “MACD histogram” does not refer to a statistical distribution here.
messages.html.087: EMA 12 = 110, EMA 26 = 105: MACD = 5. If the signal is 4, the histogram is 1. These values have the series’ unit; their magnitudes cannot be compared directly across assets with very different price levels.
messages.html.088: RSI · Relative strength of gains and losses
messages.html.089:
RS = average gain / average loss
RSI = 100 − 100 / (1 + RS)
messages.html.090: Gains are positive changes between two months; losses are the absolute values of negative changes. The application initialises their averages over N changes, then uses Wilder’s smoothing: new average = [(N − 1) × previous average + new change] / N. The default period is 14 months.
messages.html.091: Average gain = 2 and average loss = 1: RS = 2 and RSI ≈ 66.7. With no losses, RSI is 100; with no gains, it is 0. If both averages are zero, the application displays 50.
messages.html.092: The usual reference levels are 70 (“overbought”) and 30 (“oversold”). They describe a recent imbalance: a high RSI can persist during an uptrend. These empirical thresholds do not, by themselves, predict a reversal.
messages.html.095:
σann(t) = √12 × s(ℓt−n+1, …, ℓt)
Displayed value in % = 100 × σann(t)
messages.html.096: This measures the dispersion of logarithmic returns over a rolling window, 12 months by default. High volatility means changes are more dispersed, both upwards and downwards. It does not indicate their direction.
messages.html.097: Annualisation by √12 corresponds to adding monthly variances under the assumption of uncorrelated returns and stable variance. It remains an estimation convention, not a direct measurement of observed annual returns.
messages.html.098: A monthly standard deviation of 2% gives an annualised volatility of approximately 2 × √12 = 6.93%.
messages.html.099: Why can the curve respond with a lag?
messages.html.100: Each new month enters the window while the oldest leaves it. A shock can increase dispersion immediately and continue to influence the indicator until it leaves the window. Smoothing can extend or shift a peak: the curve describes movements already observed.
messages.html.101: The document proposes relative regimes: calm below the first quartile Q₁, intermediate between Q₁ and Q₃, and turbulent above Q₃. These thresholds depend on the selected history; quartile zones are not plotted in this version of the application.
messages.html.104: A weakly stationary series has a constant mean and variance over time, with covariance depending on the time lag. A price level may drift persistently, while its changes may behave more stably.
messages.html.105:
Difference of log prices:
ln(Pt) − ln(Pt−1) = ℓt
messages.html.106: The document uses the analogy of an accumulated signal: log price resembles accumulated changes; its difference is a kind of discrete derivative. Differencing may remove a unit root without guaranteeing that all properties of the series become stable.
messages.html.108: The null hypothesis is the presence of a unit root. At the 5% significance level, a p-value below 0.05 leads to rejecting this hypothesis under the chosen specification. A higher p-value means it is not rejected; it does not prove non-stationarity.
messages.html.109: The choice of a constant, a trend and the number of lags matters for interpretation. ADF does not validate the RSI thresholds of 30 and 70.
messages.html.110: This concept is explained to follow the original document’s progression. The ADF test is available in the original Python script but is not computed here: no p-value is displayed.
messages.html.114:
CAGR = (PT / P0)1 / nyears − 1
nyears = elapsed number of months / 12
messages.html.115: CAGR is the constant rate that would link the first price to the last through compounding. It summarises the starting and ending points without describing fluctuations along the way. With only one observation, it is undefined.
messages.html.116: To grow from 100 to 200 in five years: 2<sup>1/5</sup> − 1 ≈ 14.87% per year. Over ten years: 2<sup>1/10</sup> − 1 ≈ 7.18% per year. These equivalent rates do not mean that every year achieved this growth.
messages.html.118: σ<sub>historical</sub> = √12 × s(ℓ over the selected period)
messages.html.119: The card provides one measure for the selected period; the rolling curve shows local changes over time. At least two returns, hence three prices, are needed to calculate this sample standard deviation.
messages.html.120: The interpretation “approximately 68% within one standard deviation” assumes an appropriate Gaussian distribution. It is not guaranteed coverage for financial returns or an automatic consequence of annualisation.
messages.html.122:
Peakt = max(P0, …, Pt)
Drawdownt = Pt / Peakt − 1
MDD = min(Drawdownt)
messages.html.123: Maximum drawdown measures the largest decline from a peak to a subsequent trough within the period. It is zero or negative under the application’s convention. Unlike volatility, it focuses only on losses from a peak.
messages.html.124: 100 → 120 → 90 → 130: the total change is +30%, but the worst decline is 90 / 120 − 1 = −25%. Positive final performance does not erase this intermediate loss.
messages.html.125: Because observations are monthly, troughs between two points are not measured. This historical maximum loss is not an upper bound on future losses.
messages.html.133: Returns between visible prices; no return preceding the first month.
messages.html.135: Complete windows that may start before the first visible month.
messages.html.137: All available history up to the month being calculated, followed by the display filter.
messages.html.138: EMA starts at the first price. RSI waits for N changes and then uses Wilder’s smoothing. A 12-month SMA needs 12 prices; 12-month volatility needs 12 returns, hence 13 prices. Values without sufficient history remain blank. No future observation enters these calculations.
messages.html.139: Base 100 transforms the price and overlaid curves. The logarithmic axis retains their values and units but changes the vertical spacing of ticks. Neither choice changes RSI, MACD or the cards. A zero or negative Bollinger bound cannot be represented on a logarithmic axis; the band is interrupted there. The linear scale includes zero by default; “Data range” provides a more detailed view.
messages.html.140: Imports must be continuous, without duplicates, with positive prices. Applied INSEE histories are saved in the browser when storage is available. Settings and personal CSV imports last for the session. Indicators exclude fees, taxes and distributed income.
messages.html.142: This guide follows Tools for analysing a price series by Louis Tomczyk, source tex/main.tex, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0. Formulas use no external dependencies so they remain readable offline.
messages.html.143: Several interpretations have been clarified: the MACD histogram is a difference, ADF does not validate RSI thresholds, and drawdown follows an always non-positive convention. The document’s unsourced crisis tables and numerical ranges are not reproduced; the examples above illustrate calculations.

messages.html.159: In the project folder, run python3 outils/actualiser_cours.py --serve, then open http://127.0.0.1:8765. No Python packages to install. Stop the service with Ctrl+C.
messages.html.160: When opening the HTML file by double-clicking, use “Import a JSON data package”. To create one, run python3 outils/actualiser_cours.py. The file is stored in a dated subfolder of mises_a_jour/.
messages.html.161: Data are retrieved on request. Applied histories are saved in the browser when storage is available. Also save the complete JSON to transfer or restore them after clearing storage. Analysis and imports work offline.
messages.html.163: INSEE is the statistical publisher used here; it provides monthly reference-price series. A spot price, a fixing, a futures contract and an index are not interchangeable. These series do not provide real-time quotes.
messages.html.167: US dollars per ounce → USD / troy oz
messages.html.169: US cents per troy ounce → USD / troy oz (divided by 100)

messages.html.174: To find other series, use the INSEE index and time-series catalogue. Note the idBank identifier, title, currency, unit, frequency and series status before downloading its history.
messages.html.175: 010002091 (Brent) and 010002094 (copper) are euro-based indices with base year 2010, not dollar prices. The collector uses the price series listed above. Silver normalisation applies only to officially retrieved data, never to old CSV files whose units have not been established.
messages.html.178: To trace market references or cross-check an observation, also consult:
messages.html.179: ICE Benchmark Administration · LBMA Precious Metals: precious-metal benchmarks. The LBMA historical tables are accessed through a portal; access and reuse may require a licence.
messages.html.180: London Metal Exchange · Copper: copper prices and references. Distinguish spot prices, three-month delivery and monthly averages. Check the terms for accessing historical data.
messages.html.181: U.S. Energy Information Administration · Europe Brent Spot Price FOB: a monthly series in dollars per barrel, useful for cross-checking. A different provider or aggregation method may yield a different value.
messages.html.182: These links support research and verification. The built-in automated collector uses INSEE only.
messages.html.184: Query the source. An HTTPS request to the INSEE public SDMX service requests all four complete series, without startPeriod or lastNObservations.
messages.html.185: Validate the content. Identifiers, monthly frequency, unit and multiplier are checked. Non-positive prices, duplicates and internal gaps cause retrieval to fail. Missing observations at the edges are excluded and recorded.
messages.html.186: Normalise. Silver values in US cents are converted to dollars; no other conversion or interpolation is performed.
messages.html.187: Preview changes. The complete merged period and differences are displayed. “Use these data” applies all four series together without deleting months missing from the new retrieval.
messages.html.188: Retain provenance. The service archives raw XML and dated JSON, then updates historique_complet.json while retaining existing months. SHA-256 identifies the latest raw XML, not the merged data. Original CSV files remain intact.
messages.html.189: The retrieval date is not the price observation month. A successful retrieval may add no new month. The latest published month appears in the preview; an old series is not labelled “real time”.
messages.html.190: Why not extract HTML pages directly?
messages.html.191: Pages change structure and may require JavaScript. Their APIs and download files offer a more stable interface. The small local service retrieves data for the browser without depending on cross-site reading permissions (CORS).
messages.html.192: To add a site without an API, create a source-specific adapter: check access conditions and robots.txt, retrieve only the relevant public table, identify columns and units, then apply the same validation. Save the raw response and test extraction against a known copy. Do not bypass login, CAPTCHA or paid access; generic extraction from arbitrary sites is not enabled.
messages.html.194: A network error, an unexpected response or a unit change leaves current series intact. Consult the INSEE series page and try again later, or import a previously saved JSON data package. An identifier change must be checked and reflected in the collector catalogue; series are never silently substituted.
messages.html.196: CSV with columns date,prix (or date,price), dates YYYY-MM. Commas, semicolons or tabs are accepted. INSEE “valeurs_mensuelles.csv” exports are also accepted after extracting the ZIP file. Specify the published unit: this CSV import does not convert cents to dollars. For normalised units, use the JSON data package in “Sources & updates”. The import replaces the selected asset for this session.

messages.archive.title: Embedded histories · provenance and data copies
messages.archive.intro: Original data retained without currency conversion. USGS: annual metal unit values since 1900, in current dollars per metric tonne. EIA: annual U.S. oil prices since 1859. World Bank: monthly series since 1960.
messages.archive.note: All these histories are embedded and available in Analysis on opening. The series selector only chooses what is displayed. Frequencies, units and definitions remain distinct; no currency conversion or merging of providers is applied.
messages.series.select: Series to analyse — all histories are already loaded
messages.series.annual: Each point represents the stated year, not a month or a year-end close. Points are placed at mid-year for display. Indicator windows are in years; volatility uses √1. Returns and drawdowns refer to annual averages and do not describe within-year fluctuations. Lines connect observations without creating monthly data.
messages.series.monthly: Each point represents a month. Indicator windows are in months and volatility uses √12. Each provider retains its own series; sources are never spliced automatically.
messages.series.ratio: Ratio of the two monthly INSEE series normalised to dollars per troy ounce.
messages.meaning.usgs_or: USGS · Gold · current USD per metric tonne. Annual unit value estimated from the average world market price in 1900–1967, then the average Engelhard quotation for refined gold from 1968. This is not a December 31 close. The note does not specify the exact observation calendar or weighting of each average.
messages.meaning.usgs_argent: USGS · Silver · current USD per metric tonne. Annual average value per tonne of silver with a minimum purity of 99.9%. Sources: Metal Prices through 1998 for 1900–1998, then Minerals Yearbook. This is not a year-end close; the note does not detail the exact observation weighting.
messages.meaning.usgs_cuivre: USGS · Copper · current USD per metric tonne. Unit value estimated using the Annual Average U.S. Producer Copper Price. This is neither an LME quotation nor a December 31 close. The note does not specify the exact weighting of the average.
messages.meaning.eia_petrole_us: EIA · U.S. crude oil · annual average first purchase price, USD per barrel. This U.S. reference goes back to 1859 and is distinct from Brent. Definitions and collection methods have evolved over this history.
messages.meaning.wb_or: World Bank · monthly average of the London afternoon fixing, 99.5% fine gold, USD per troy ounce.
messages.meaning.wb_argent: World Bank · silver, USD per troy ounce. London fixing; Handy & Harman before July 1976, unrefined silver before 1962. These definition changes are explicitly retained.
messages.meaning.wb_cuivre: World Bank · LME grade A copper, settlement price, USD per metric tonne; monthly observations.
messages.meaning.wb_brent: World Bank · Crude oil, Brent column, USD per barrel. Values before 1976 predate production at the Brent field; their historical construction still needs verification. This series is displayed separately without splicing to INSEE.
messages.meaning.insee: Monthly INSEE series or imported CSV. Units and provenance are those stated for the series; personal CSV imports are not converted automatically.
messages.chart.volInfo.annual: Standard deviation over {months} years · annual factor √1
messages.html.212.annual: Circles: yearly observations; lines: connections between points. Averages use distinct dash patterns. SVG: vector figure with axes, units and legend.
